en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Book of Puzzles,
Chapter on Familiarity.
9. The Question Concerning Food Chanted with Verses “Venerable Nāgasena, this has been said by the Blessed One:
‘Food chanted with verses is not to be eaten by me.’”
“O Brahmin, this is not the Dhamma for those who see clearly;
the Buddhas reject verses sung as praise.
When the Dhamma exists, O Brahmin, such is the proper conduct.”
Furthermore, when the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma to an assembly, he first delivers a gradual discourse, beginning with a talk on generosity and followed by a talk on virtuous conduct.
Having heard the words of that Blessed One, the Lord of the Entire World, gods and humans prepare and give gifts;
his disciples then enjoy those gifts which were offered for his sake.
“Venerable Nāgasena, if it was spoken by the Blessed One:
‘Song to the accompaniment of verses is not fit to be eaten by me,’ then that statement, ‘The Blessed One first delivers a discourse on giving,’ must be false.
If he first delivers a discourse on giving, then that statement, ‘Song to the accompaniment of verses is not fit to be eaten by me,’ must also be false.”
What is the reason for this?

Venerable sir, when that person worthy of offerings explains the result of householders’ gift of almsfood, those who hear his discourse on the Dhamma give gifts again and again with a confident heart. And all those who consume that gift consume it accompanied by verses of song.
“This too is a subtle and profound double-pronged question that has come to you; it must be resolved by you.
“Great King, this was indeed spoken by the Blessed One:
‘Song-chanted verse is not fit to be eaten by me; O Brahmin, for those who see clearly, this is not the Dhamma.’”
"Buddhas reject songs sung to them; this is the way of the Dhamma, O Brahmin," so it is said.
And the Blessed One first gives a talk on giving; for that is the practice of all Tathāgatas:
having first made the mind delighted there by a talk on giving, they subsequently enjoin one to virtue.
Just as, Great King, people first give playthings to their young children—
namely, a bow, a top,
a spinning-top, a cart, a chariot, and a bow— and afterwards employ them each in their own respective tasks.
In the same way, Great King, the Tathāgata first delights the mind with a discourse on giving and afterwards enjoins it upon virtue.
Or again, Great King, just as a physician first has his patients drink oil for four or five days to strengthen them and soften them, and afterwards administers a purgative;
even so, Great King, the Tathāgata first delights the mind with a discourse on giving and afterwards enjoins it upon virtue.
“Great King, the minds of donors and masters of giving become supple, gentle, and tender;
by means of that bridge of giving and the ship of giving, they cross to the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra.
Therefore, he first instructs them in the field of action, yet he does not make a request of anyone.”
“Venerable Nāgasena, regarding what you say is ‘intimation’ (viññatti), how many kinds of intimation are there?
“There are two kinds of intimation, Great King: bodily intimation and verbal intimation.
Among these, there is bodily intimation that is blameworthy and there is that which is blameless.”
There is verbal intimation that is blameworthy, and there is that which is blameless.
What is bodily intimation that is blameworthy?
Here, a certain bhikkhu, having approached families, stands in a place where he has no right of way and obstructs the path; this is bodily intimation that is blameworthy.

And what is requested by her the Noble Ones do not consume; furthermore, that person is despised, scorned, ridiculed, censured, treated with contempt, and disregarded in the presence of the Noble Ones, and is reckoned as one of "broken livelihood.

Again, Great King, suppose here a certain bhikkhu, having approached families, stands in an improper place and, having extended his neck, looks with a peacock’s glance, thinking, "In this way they will look at me," and they indeed look at him in that way—this too is a bodily intimation.
It is blameworthy, and the Noble Ones do not partake of what has been requested by such a person;

furthermore, that individual is held in contempt, despised, ridiculed, censured, treated with disregard, and disregarded by the Noble Ones in accordance with their doctrine, and he comes to be known simply as one of "broken livelihood.
Furthermore, Great King, here some bhikkhu [uses] his jaw, or his brow, or his thumb...
If one makes such a request, this bodily intimation is also blameworthy; and what has been requested by means of it, the Noble Ones do not consume.

Furthermore, that person is held in low esteem, despised, scorned, censured, and treated with contempt by the Noble Ones according to their standard, and is reckoned as one whose livelihood is broken.
What is blameless bodily intimation?

Here, a bhikkhu, having approached families, being mindful, concentrated, and clearly comprehending, goes according to the instruction whether to a proper place or an improper place; he stands where it is proper to stand, he stands where those who wish to give are present, and he departs from where they do not wish to give.

This is blameless bodily intimation. And what is intimated by it, the Noble Ones partake of; and that person is praised, extolled, and commended in the discipline of the Noble Ones as one whose conduct is austere and whose livelihood is entirely pure. This is reckoned as such.
This too was said, Great King, by the Blessed One, the God above Gods:
“The wise do not beg;
the steadfast one deserves to know.”
"The Noble Ones stand for what has been intended;
this is the request of the Noble Ones.
What is verbal intimation that is blameworthy?
In this case, great king, a bhikkhu makes various verbal requests for robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
this verbal intimation is blameworthy, and what is requested by it is not used by the noble ones.

Furthermore, that person is despised, scorned, derided, censured, treated with contempt, and disregarded by the noble ones in accordance with their doctrine, and he is reckoned as one whose livelihood is broken.
Furthermore, Great King, here a certain bhikkhu, soliciting from others, says:
"I have need of this. If, by that speech of his soliciting others, gain arises for him, this intimation by speech is blameworthy;
and what is thus intimated by it is not used by the Noble Ones, and that person stands outside the doctrine of the Noble Ones.
He is recognized as one who is despised, reviled, mocked, censured, treated with contempt, and disregarded; he indeed comes to be known as one of "broken livelihood.
Furthermore, Great King, here some bhikkhu makes himself heard by the assembly through a gesture of his speech, saying, "In such and such a way should gifts be given to the bhikkhus";
and having heard those words of his, they bring forth what has been praised. This too—

Verbal intimation is blameworthy; what is intimated by it the Noble Ones do not consume, and that person is despised, scorned, reviled, censured, treated with contempt, and disregarded in the discipline of the Noble Ones, and is reckoned as one of "broken livelihood.

Is it not true, Great King, that even the Elder Sāriputta, when he was ill during the night after the sun had set, broke his silence when questioned about medicine by the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, and through that breaking of speech, the medicine was obtained for him?

Then the Elder Sāriputta, thinking, “This medicine has been obtained by me through verbal intimation; let not my livelihood be destroyed,” abandoned that medicine out of fear for the destruction of his livelihood and did not use it.
Thus, too, verbal intimation is blameworthy, and what is intimated by it the Noble Ones do not consume.

Furthermore, such a person is despised, scorned, ridiculed, censured, treated with contempt, and disregarded according to the standard of the Noble Ones; he is reckoned simply as one whose livelihood is broken.
What is blameless verbal intimation?
Here, Great King, a bhikkhu, when there is a requisite, requests medicine from families that have been invited by his relatives;
this is blameless verbal intimation. And the Noble Ones consume what has been requested by him, and that person [is pleasing] to the Noble Ones.
At that time, he was praised, extolled, and lauded; he came to be known as one of pure livelihood, approved by the Tathāgatas, the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
But as for the reason, Great King, why the Tathāgata rejected the food of the brahmin Kasībhāradvāja—
“It arose through the binding, unbinding, pulling, and restraining [of the earth], and therefore the Tathāgata rejected that alms-food and did not subsist upon it.

“Venerable Nāgasena, at all times when the Tathāgata was eating, did the deities scatter divine essence into his bowl, or did they scatter it only during those two specific alms-meals, namely the ‘pig’s delight’ and the honey-milk porridge?”
“Great King, at all times while the Tathāgata is eating, deities take divine nutritive essence (*ojā*) and, standing nearby, sprinkle it over each morsel as it is lifted.
Just as, Great King, a king’s cook, when the king is eating, takes broth and stands by, sprinkling the broth over each mouthful;
even so, Great King, at all times while the Tathāgata is eating, deities take divine nutritive essence and, standing nearby, sprinkle divine nutritive essence over each morsel as it is lifted.”

“Even at Verañjā, Great King, while the Tathāgata was eating coarse barley meal, the deities, having moistened it again and again with divine nutritive essence (*ojā*), offered it to him; by that means, the Tathāgata’s body became nourished.
“It is indeed a gain for those deities, venerable Nāgasena, who were constantly and continuously intent upon attending to the Tathāgata’s person.
Well said, venerable Nāgasena! It is so; I accept it as such.”
The ninth question: On food sung to the accompaniment of verses.
